query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The formation and crystal-structure selection of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the mixing entropy and partial pressure of the constituent elements in the vapor phase, which can be controlled by adjusting the composition and processing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Mixture of pure elemental metal powders
generation.intervention: Continuous synthesis using a thermal plasma jet with controlled plasma gases and feed rate
generation.conditions: High-temperature (>8000 K) and high-speed plasma jet, rapid quenching, and ultrahigh cooling rate (10^5 - 10^6 K s^-1)
generation.structural_mediator: Homogeneous multicomponent vapor and co-nucleation process
generation.mechanism: Mixing entropy and partial pressure of constituent elements control the nucleation and growth of nanoparticles
generation.predicted_outcome: Formation of single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles with uniform composition and crystal structure
generation.baseline: Conventional alloy synthesis methods with phase separation and elemental segregation
generation.boundary: Compositional boundaries: equimolar ratio of constituent elements; Processing boundaries: plasma power, feed rate, and plasma gas composition
generation.uncertainty: Effects of plasma gas composition and feed rate on nanoparticle growth and composition

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize nanoparticles using a thermal plasma jet with varying plasma gas compositions and feed rates, and characterize their composition and crystal structure
measurements: Energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy elemental mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles exhibit phase separation or elemental segregation, the hypothesis is falsified

Although the CTS technique has demonstrated a remarkable potential in synthesizing HEA NPs in a controlled manner, the process is limited to electrically conductive supports and operated in a batch mode, thus not suitable for industrial-scale production of HEA NPs. To overcome this challenge, new methods building on the CTS technique were reported, such as microwave heating, fast moving bed pyrolysis, and aerosol methods. Very recently, a pulsed/scanning laser ablation method was also reported and demonstrated synthesis of high-entropy materials on various substrates. However, the feedstock is typically limited to metal salts. The vapor-source technique also provides a very effective way to form alloy NPs. In this approach, a well-mixed vapor comprising multiple elements is formed from the vaporization of pure metal feedstock, and then rapidly quenched to form crystal solids. Here, in a proof-of-concept demonstration, we report the synthesis of CrFeCoNiMo HEA NPs with an average size of 50 nm at a high rate approaching 35 g h−1 using an inductively coupled plasma jet (ICPJ). Despite the low saturation pressure of Mo, all metal elements in a particle are homogeneously mixed at the atomic level with good crystallinity. It is discussed that mixing multiple elements at a near equimolar ratio not only increases the mixing entropy but also decreases the partial pressure of the constituent element (i.e., Pi = Ptotal / N, where Pi is the partial pressure of ith constituent element, Ptotal is the total pressure, and N is the total number of the constituent elements) in the vapor, which prohibits the continuous growth of nuclei into pure metal particles via homogenous condensation. The final HEA NPs formed are continuously collected by a porous filter unit at a high yield rate of ~35 g h−1, while unvaporized feedstock is removed from the reaction stream by a cyclone separator.
To ensure the compositional uniformity, unlike the conventional alloy (Fig. 1b), it would be ideal that all the constituent elements in the vapor nucleates simultaneously by co-nucleation process (i.e., nucleation by multicomponent), followed by co-condensation of metal monomers onto the nuclei formed (Fig. 1c). However, the nucleation temperature of a metal vapor strongly depends on its saturation vapor pressure - an intrinsic property of an element. This presents a potential challenge in the synthesis of HEA NPs from the direct vaporization of metal powders by a plasma jet. As a proof-of-concept demonstration, we have studied a Cr-Fe-Co-Ni-Mo system where Mo exhibits a significantly different nucleation temperature compared with other elements, and discussed the growth mechanism. The thermal plasma process is usually accompanied by the production of impurities from incomplete vaporization of feedstock because a fraction of the feedstock injected typically bounces back from the plasma core. This has also been prevalent in the ICPJ process due to the elevated viscosity near the plasma core (e.g., 10 times higher than at room temperature) and the presence of recirculation eddies formed by the magnetic pinch.
